issues.legal_issue: Retrospective legislation may constitutionally validate eviction actions taken under an earlier public-premises law by making those actions subject to a replacement law that removes the discriminatory choice between eviction procedures.
material_facts: Eviction orders were made against the occupants under the earlier public-premises law, and appeals from those orders were pending when the replacement law was enacted.

The replacement law applied retrospectively, deemed actions taken under the earlier law to have been taken under its corresponding provisions, and barred courts from entertaining eviction proceedings concerning unauthorised occupation of public premises.
The replacement law provided a single eviction procedure; the procedure, including the right of appeal, was materially the same as the procedure used in the cases.
issues.conclusion: The retrospective replacement law was constitutionally valid, and the earlier eviction actions were to be tested under its provisions; the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 14 of the Constitution, the vice identified in Northern India Caterers Private Ltd. v. State of Punjab, [1967] 3 SCR 399, arose from the availability of both a special eviction procedure and an ordinary-court procedure without guidance for choosing between them. A legislature competent to regulate eviction from public premises may legislate retrospectively and remove that vice by leaving only one procedure. A validating law is sustained where the legislature has competence over the subject and removes the defect identified in the earlier law. The Court relied on M/s West Ramnad Electric Distribution Co. Ltd. v. State of Madras, [1963] 2 SCR 747, distinguishing Deputy Commissioner and Collector, Kamrup v. Durga Nath Sarma, [1968] 1 SCR 561; it also relied on State of Mysore v. D. Achiah Chetty, [1963] 3 SCR 55, and referred to Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality, [1970] 1 SCR 388. The relevant provisions were sections 15 and 20 of the 1971 Act and section 5 of the 1958 Act. Beg J. additionally observed that the 1958 Act had not itself been declared unconstitutional and that the earlier procedure had to satisfy the replacement law's requirements.

predicates.appeal_challenges_eviction_under_earlier: An appeal challenges an eviction action taken under an earlier law governing public premises.
predicates.replacement_law_applies_retroactively: A later law governing eviction from public premises is made applicable to a period that includes the earlier action.
predicates.past_actions_are_deemed_taken_under_repl: The later law treats actions taken under the earlier law as actions taken under its corresponding provisions.
predicates.replacement_law_leaves_one_eviction_proc: The later law leaves a single procedure for evicting unauthorised occupants of public premises rather than a choice between that procedure and an ordinary-court procedure.
predicates.legislature_has_authority_over_public_pr: The legislature has authority to regulate eviction of unauthorised occupants from public premises.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an earlier public-premises eviction action, a retrospective replacement law deems the action to have been taken under its provisions, leaves one eviction procedure, and is within legislative authority, the action is effective if it satisfies that replacement law.

issues.legal_issue: Agricultural land is included within the scope of a law governing eviction from public premises when the law defines premises to include any land.
material_facts: The appellants were in unauthorised occupation of agricultural land belonging to the Government.
The governing law defined premises to include any land and contained no exclusion for agricultural land.
issues.conclusion: The agricultural land fell within the law's definition of premises, and the occupant could be evicted under that law.
issues.legal_principle: The ordinary breadth of the definition of premises as including any land encompasses agricultural land; the Court found no statutory exclusion. The Court also rejected the contention that the legislation was outside the central legislature's competence, holding that the legislature could provide a speedy procedure for eviction from public premises. The relevant provisions were the definition of premises in section 2 and the eviction procedure in the 1971 Act.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding_concerns_public_premises and occupant_is_in_unauthorized_possession and property_is_agricultural_land and governing_definition_includes_any_land and no_agricultural_land_exclusion_applies

predicates.eviction_proceeding_concerns_public_prem: An eviction proceeding concerns premises belonging to, leased by, or requisitioned on behalf of a public authority covered by the governing law.
predicates.occupant_is_in_unauthorized_possession: The occupant has no authority to occupy the public premises or continues in occupation after that authority has ended.
predicates.property_is_agricultural_land: The property in dispute is land used for agriculture.
predicates.governing_definition_includes_any_land: The governing law defines premises broadly to include any land.
predicates.no_agricultural_land_exclusion_applies: The governing law does not exclude agricultural land from its coverage.

issues.definition: If unauthorised occupation of public premises is at issue, the property is agricultural land, and the governing definition includes any land without excluding agricultural land, the agricultural land is within the eviction law's scope.

issues.legal_issue: The availability of a separate tenancy-law procedure for ejectment does not make a public-premises eviction procedure discriminatory when the public-premises law itself provides only one procedure.
material_facts: The appellants relied on the availability of ejectment procedures under sections 42 and 43 of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887.
The replacement public-premises law provided one procedure for ejecting unauthorised occupants of public premises and barred court proceedings in respect of that eviction.
issues.conclusion: The availability of the tenancy-law procedure did not make the public-premises eviction procedure discriminatory under Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 is not infringed on this ground where the public-premises law provides only one procedure for ejectment; the existence of a procedure under the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887, does not create the choice between alternative procedures under the public-premises law that had produced the discrimination identified in Northern India Caterers Private Ltd. v. State of Punjab, [1967] 3 SCR 399. The Court relied on sections 15 and 20 of the 1971 Act and considered sections 42 and 43 of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887.

predicates.challenge_is_to_public_premises_eviction: A party challenges the procedure used to evict an unauthorised occupant from public premises.
predicates.public_premises_law_provides_one_evictio: The public-premises law provides only one procedure for ejectment of unauthorised occupants.
predicates.separate_tenancy_ejectment_procedure_is_: A separate law provides a procedure for ejectment in tenancy matters.

issues.definition: If a challenge concerns a public-premises eviction law that provides one eviction procedure, the existence of a separate tenancy ejectment procedure does not make the public-premises scheme discriminatory.
